summary: Lists the goals for SMIng, a proposed new data definition language for modeling network management information that could map to SNMP and COPS-PR operations. It sets objectives rather than defining the language itself. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a new language for describing network equipment, people wrote down what it should be able to do. This is that wish list.

questions: what was smi next generation meant to do
subtitle: Design objectives for a unified data definition language for network management.

tldr.problem: Network management uses incompatible data definition languages (SMIv2 for SNMP and SPPI for COPS-PR), and the SMI specification has known limitations in expressiveness and completeness for modern management needs.
tldr.mechanism: SMIng (SMI Next Generation) is proposed as a unified, protocol-independent data definition language that can be mapped to multiple protocols and provides enhanced expressiveness including inheritance, attribute groups, and formal relationship definitions.
tldr.outcome: This objectives document captures working group consensus on what SMIng should accomplish, providing guidance for language designers without defining the language itself.

today: RFC 3216 is an Informational document that served as requirements input for SMIng language design. The actual SMIng language specification followed in later RFCs, allowing the community to converge on a unified data definition language for network management across multiple protocols.

sections.title: The Need for a Unified Language
sections.content:
As networking technology has evolved, network management has grown to support diverse technologies and protocols. Different standard management protocols use different data definition languages: SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2) is used with SNMP, while SPPI (Structure of Policy Provisioning Information) is used with COPS-PR. This fragmentation creates redundancy and inconsistency.

The SMIng working group was chartered to define a new, unified data definition language that eliminates the need for separate SMIv2 and SPPI specifications. Beyond unification, SMIng aims to address limitations in the current languages by providing greater expressiveness, allowing definition of concepts like table existence relationships, instance creation/deletion, and attribute group inheritance.
sections.plainLanguage: Different management systems describe network stuff in different ways. People want one language that works for all of them, and that's better at describing complex things.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
The Internet Research Task Force's Network Management Research Group (NMRG) conducted research into creating a protocol-independent data definition language usable by multiple protocols. Because SMIv2 and SPPI are very similar, the NMRG focused on merging them while researching ways to abstract the objectives for use with other protocols like LDAP and Diameter.

The fundamental motivation is to permit more expressive and complete representation of modeled information. Current languages require workarounds for concepts that should be directly expressible, such as how one table depends on the existence of rows in another table, or the ability to formally define attribute groups that can be inherited and reused across multiple protocol mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers found that these two languages are almost the same, but neither one can easily describe modern management needs. A new one should fix both problems at once.

sections.title: Core Accepted Objectives
sections.content:
The SMIng working group identified 44 accepted objectives divided into basic requirements, alignment objectives (where SMIv2 and SPPI differ), and fixes for known problems. Basic objectives include textual representation, human readability, rigorously defined syntax, mechanisms for naming and module organization, and support for base data types including Integer32, Unsigned32, Integer64, Unsigned64, Enumeration, Bits, OctetString, and OID.

Alignment objectives include features supported differently in SMIv2 versus SPPI, such as accessibility declarations (read, write, create, delete), range and size constraints, and table existence relationships using INDEX, AUGMENTS, and EXTENDS. Critical new objectives include attribute groups (named, reusable sets of attributes like C structs), single inheritance for extending attribute groups, containment relationships, and support for discriminated unions.

The group rejected objectives deemed too general or impractical, including formal attribute value constraints, transaction constraints, methods, and agent capability descriptions. The focus was on enhancing the state of art in data modeling rather than attempting to merge SMIv2 and SPPI if the two goals conflicted.
sections.plainLanguage: The new language must describe data in plain text, have clear rules, support tables and inheritance, and work for both SNMP and COPS-PR without getting too fancy.

sections.title: Protocol Independence and Mapping
sections.content:
A core objective is that SMIng definitions must be protocol-independent, allowing the same data definition to be mapped to SNMP, COPS-PR, and potentially other protocols. The language itself remains neutral, with protocol-specific details and OID assignments handled in separate protocol mapping documents.

This separation has important implications: the protocol mappings can assign OIDs (Object Identifiers) and define protocol-specific syntax, while the core language focuses purely on data modeling. It allows the same management information to be expressed in multiple protocols without forcing the language design to accommodate the specific quirks of any single protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The language describes what you want to manage, and separate documents say how to do it in SNMP or COPS-PR. This way one description works everywhere.

sections.title: Advanced Features and Language Design
sections.content:
SMIng must provide mechanisms for language extensibility, allowing future modules to contain new syntax without breaking existing parsers. It must support clear rules for extending modules without causing interoperability problems. The language must deprecate confusing features like the IMPLIED indexing keyword from SMIv2, which many people misunderstand.

Nice-to-have objectives include methods (operation signatures), float data types, internationalization of documentation, arrays (SEQUENCE OF), and clearer comment syntax (like C++/Java style). Some of these may be practical to include at language creation time to avoid future problems, such as float types which cannot be added later without changing the language fundamentally.

Rejected objectives include having the language define procedures or formal attribute value constraints, handling of agent capabilities descriptions, and mechanisms to specify associations with cardinalities between attribute groups. These were deemed too general or implementation-specific to include in a language specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The language should be easy to extend later without breaking old code. Comments should be like C++ so people understand them. Some things like float numbers should probably be added now even if not needed yet.
